utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could remind you of the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could please have D590 up on the screen and this is Defence 65 ter 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back very briefly to a document we were discussing yesterday and this is a report that was sent to you and other members of your liaison team, and it's dated 24th December - it should be 1998, but I note that the English says 1999. And this report refers to the deployment of a tank company of the reinforced 15th Armoured Brigade to the area of the Batlava airfield sector. You remember we were discussing this report yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3 in the English, the bottom, page 3; and this is page 4 in the B/C/S, also in the bottom. This is -- are we there? No. There.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There's a reference in the report to a meeting between Loncar and General Drewienkiewicz, whom we spoke about yesterday. And General Drewienkiewicz is noted as saying that he's very surprised at the deployment of strong VJ forces in the Podujevo area. He understands that the unit is carrying out exercises on the training-ground but the timing is inappropriate to the situation. He expressed fears that the so-called KLA - and I turn the page in the English and it's also the same paragraph in B/C/S - members could open fire to which VJ members would respond and this could escalate into armed conflict. And this is page 5 in the B/C/S, and it's also the top of page 4 in the English. It notes there that he's told that the training activities would last until 22nd December, so that is four days after this deployment. Do you see the passage I'm referring to, those two paragraphs there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall that this unit in fact did not leave the area of the Batlava airfield in Podujevo municipality on the 22nd, as had been announced to General Drewienkiewicz from the KVM. It in fact was reinforced with additional units. Do you recall that happening some days later?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not quite, but you can see that from this part here. From here you see that it's going to be until the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What I'm asking, sir, is this unit was in fact not sent back to barracks on the 22nd. Additional units were sent to this area by the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it here. It's possible, but I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Let me show you another document and maybe that refreshes your memory of what I'm speaking about, this is P9666 [sic], these are the VJ collegium minutes of 24th December 1998. This is in fact the same date that the report was drafted, and I'm looking for page 14 in the English, and I believe it's the same page in the B/C/S. And this is passage where Mihajlovic is speaking, and he was the leader of the duty operations of the VJ General Staff; correct? Are you familiar with General Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was the acting duty operations officer, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And in the passage he starts speaking at the previous page, but this passage is -- it's on the top page of the English, if we could scroll back to the top page of the English. It says: "One fortified tank company went out for training on 19th December, and two mechanised platoons from the 15th Armoured Brigade on the 22nd of December. They were combined to form provisional formations in the area of the Batlava airport ..." and it goes on to indicate the composition. And it says in total there are 221 persons, there are also nine tanks, T-55 tanks, ten M-80 combat vehicles, three Pragas, one armoured personnel carrier, three mortars, and one tank. Do you recall the fact that these units were sent, these additional reinforcements were sent to the area of Batlava on this date? And we're speaking of the date on which the unit was supposed to pull out from the area, that's on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't have to be a reinforcement. These can be other units which came to also take part in the exercise and the training.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But the information that had been provided to KVM was that the unit would be sent back to barracks, that the trainings would conclude on the 22nd; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Didn't we just look at the report that you had received which stated that that's what General Drewienkiewicz had been told in his meeting with Colonel Loncar?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we see it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can. This is D590, and the passage is page 5 in the English. I believe it's also page 5 in the B/C/S. Do you see that in the first paragraph, the date of 22nd?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it now. I see it now. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So what I'm asking, sir, if this unit in fact was reinforced and was not withdrawn from the area, as had been announced to the KVM -- in fact, remained in the area and was reinforced?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably remained in the area for some time until the planned exercises were finished, but General Loncar was not a representative of the army. So he was not really in close contact in relation to these assignments, so it's possible that this was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that on the days following this VJ collegium meeting that we just referred to, that was the 24th of December, fighting broke out in the area where these units were deployed in the -- near the Batlava airfield and the Podujevo municipality? And this was fighting between the VJ and MUP and KLA forces. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I wasn't really following those activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Wouldn't this have been included in the daily reports you were receiving from the 3rd Army command liaison officer in the section on incidents affecting the VJ? Wouldn't this be the type of information reported in these daily reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably, but I don't really recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you don't recall hearing anything about this from other members of your liaison team?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that now, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you don't recall hearing about anything from any members of the KVM or any complaints from the KVM regarding this incident I'm referring to, the fighting in this area? You don't recall anything about that either?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our team. I don't know if this was in some other place. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I must say, sir, I'm quite surprised that you weren't aware of this, as news of this incident made it all the way back to Belgrade. I now want to show you a document, this is P1330, it's dated 30th of December, 1998. And if we could have page 14 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S. And these are the VJ -- the minutes of the VJ collegium of that date, as we see when the page has been displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm looking for page 14 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a passage that starts on the previous page in the English, and on the B/C/S we have it on the same page. And it's General Dimitrijevic speaking. I take it, sir, you're familiar with General Dimitrijevic, he was the chief of the army security at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, but I do know that he was the chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could scroll up in the English. I think we've moved down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to a passage that starts: "In addition, the current situation in the vicinity of Podujevo, I think that we must be completely consistent here and completely open towards each other, so to speak. The situation in Podujevo and the surroundings, it was complex before, but when did it suddenly become even more complicated? After the so-called --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "... after the so-called pretend or real planned exercises in which this company took part in the field. "General, these sorts of moves will lead us to disaster, the explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do. The fact that the MUP did not do what it had to do afterwards has resulted in what we have now." Do you see the passage I just read out, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, sir, based on your knowledge of the agreement which we went over yesterday, that this sort of deployment under the pretext of an exercise would in fact have been a violation of the obligations of the VJ under these agreements?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't come to that conclusion. First of all, I'm not aware of these reports from the collegium sessions, and you know that I did not attend those meetings of the collegium. Secondly, I don't know what the other senior officers noted in respect of this comment by Mr. Dimitrijevic. It would be interesting to hear the comment of the Chief of the General Staff. But I would like to say something. We in the team --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, if I can stop you there. I'm not asking whether you heard these comments personally or I'm not suggesting that you were at this meeting. All I'm asking is based on your knowledge of the agreements we went over yesterday if a deployment of this type, which is a unit being deployed outside of barracks under the pretext of a planning -- of a training exercise but really to draw fire from the KLA, if that sort of deployment was in violation of the agreements? That's what I'm asking. So I'm asking if based on your knowledge of the agreements this sort of deployment would have been a violation of the agreements?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must complete what I wanted to say. As far as we're concerned in the team, what is important to us is the report by the team signed by General Mladenovic, who was a proper officer. So I don't know about this particular one, I cannot really comment in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I note you're not really answering my question, sir, but I'll move on from that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We scroll down on the same page in the English, and it's -- I believe it's the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that General Obradovic, your team leader, is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could scroll down and scroll down in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There's a passage which begins: "We have registered it, and we have managed to avoid registering it as a combat group, because it has been defined as though it was going into battle. Instead we have registered it as some sort of mixed or mechanised company that is on extended combat training in this training-ground, and this is how it will be decided down there. That's all." And I know you haven't read the entirety of this text, but I put to you, sir, that he's speaking about the same company that was deployed in the Podujevo area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm waiting, though, for the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the text on the screen. This is all I wanted to say, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The screen is not showing that section of the text in the Serbian, so that the witness could read it. This is all I wished to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's on the next page in the B/C/S. Yes, on the top part, it's right there, right above where Colonel Zivanovic starts speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you see the passage that I've just referred to which start with: "We have registered it, and we have managed to avoid registering it as a combat group ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I think we have the right passage now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, General Obradovic here is referring to this combat group having been registered as being -- as a company on extended combat training. Who would normally register this sort of group or company as being in extended combat training? Was that something that was done at your level, at the level of your liaison group, or was this done at the level of the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps? Who would normally register it as a company on extended combat training?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, all the definitions are at the level of the army command and the corps command. We did not define anything. All we had was we received reports. We were not authorised to change anything. We received reports and we trusted our superiors. They wrote reports on behalf of the team and in agreement with the command. Nothing was done. The team was subordinated to the corps command or the army command, the 3rd Army command. So everything that was done was done in accordance with the position, the joint position, and pursuant to the correct methodology.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when it says "we have registered," does this mean that it was registered with the KVM as being a company on extended combat training? Is that what it's referring to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because General Obradovic never presented those positions from the collegium in this way, and he was not obliged to present to us the positions taken at the collegium. These are professional questions, although in this particular instance the question of relations with the missions is also being mentioned. But again, I mention we were not present. Had the general mentioned it to us, we would have acted pursuant to whatever he told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can look at another document, and this is D008-0142.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, this company or this unit that we've been referring to in the Podujevo area, they in fact did not return to barracks in January either. They were still deployed in that area; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I would have to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can look at this document. It's Defence 65 ter 781, and if we see a paragraph that starts with: "Between 0800 and 01400 hours on 27th January, a reinforced TC," which we saw in the other document was tank company; it's been translated as armoured squadron, "of the 15th Armoured Brigade was made up of 11 b/v and 69 men carried out a tactical exercise on the Pristina village of Luzane axis," and it says, "(general Podujevo sector) on the topic of securing roads and capturing assigned facilities." This is the same tank company as the 15th Armoured Brigade that we've been referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can conclude that on the basis of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that this is a regular weekly report from the period of 22nd to 28th January, and it was again sent to your liaison team. We see that at the top; correct? It's dated 28th January --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and naturally we sent the same thing to the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we can briefly turn to page 5 in the English and page 6, it's the middle of page 6 in the B/C/S. There's a reference there to a meeting which took place on the same day in the Pristina offices of the federal government's co-ordination team between General Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Dusan Loncar. And it indicates that the topic discussed at the meeting was the current situation in the general area of Podujevo and the VJ activities in the sector. Do you see the passage I'm referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These training exercises, sir, I put to you that these training exercises that this report refers to again resulted in extensive fighting in the area of Podujevo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that, but the unit did have a real reason. There was a reason to organise training there for purposes of protecting the roads, and now we see that being put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Wouldn't information on fighting in this area have been contained in the reports that you were receiving, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be usual, but there -- it's not here, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, this unit in fact remained in this area all the way until the NATO bombing campaign began in March of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the precise information. But if it did stay there it was in the training camp, and it was there at the training camp which was meant for training. But I don't know if it was there throughout that whole period. Perhaps there was some replacements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is Defence 65 ter 781. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did we have as exhibits all of the documents you put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I haven't moved to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was some problem with the recording, which is why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That should be P966. I may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: P966. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- indicated it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday when my learned colleague was questioning you, you spoke about the freedom of movement of OSCE, and that was contained in the OSCE agreement. And you indicated that the VJ understood that this freedom of movement throughout Kosovo did not include access to VJ barracks. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During the period from when the KVM was set up all the way up to the period when it withdrew from Kosovo, was it ever -- were members of the KVM ever allowed entry into VJ barracks in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and more than once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in which occasion was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were making those preparations, if you allow me a longer answer, we had ordered all these commanders to provide within the perimeter of the barracks an area so that KVM can come unhindered and wait in an area until we provide liaison officers. And since there were many such requests, we found it appropriate to receive those people and to talk to them. Many of them insisted constantly to have meetings with commanders, and they frequently did have contacts with commanders of our brigades and our border battalions. On several occasions, although I can't tell you how often, it was even allowed to them to inspect the units and the systems that they had no jurisdiction over, such as the anti-aircraft defence system, including the heavy weapons that were inspected and controlled under the agreement -- the subregional agreement on weapons control. And we accepted that the KVM should also inspect those weapons from time to time, regardless of our agreement with NATO. So there was a thaw in our relations, but simply we believed it was not entirely in keeping with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly - and I'm just also recalling your evidence from yesterday - the initial position was that access to barracks was to be denied because that was not authorised by the agreement, was that the initial position of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the initial position, with a proviso that we insisted that leaders of the mission, Ambassador Walker and his deputy Drewienkiewicz should raise the issue with political counterparts so that they should resolve the issue of entry into barracks at that level. Because the issue could expand. They could next ask to go into the apartments of the officers, and so on, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did this change in position -- you've told us that they were allowed at some point. Did this change in position happen around March of 1999? Was that when there was a change in this position and inspections into the barracks of the anti-aircraft defence system was allowed? Was that when it occurred?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a global change. It was a sign of goodwill and our readiness to co-operate even beyond our obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking if this sign of goodwill, as you've termed it, if this happened around March of 1999. You told us yesterday that this was a sticking point, and it was repeatedly raised in your meetings with KVM. Was this access to the barracks, in the way you've described it, allowed as of March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was actually a bit earlier. Yesterday in my evidence I kept trying to explain that we always had an increasingly tolerant position towards the KVM, because they were people too. There were 2.000 of them. They needed to do certain things. They needed to be engaged. It was a lot, 2.000 men, in such a small area. We knew that they were our colleagues, officers, and we had understanding for them, although I must say they did not have that much understanding for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, sir. I'll move on from there. I just have one last document I want to show you. And this is Prosecution 65 ter 01473, if we could have that up on the screen. And yesterday, sir, while that is being brought up you told us that you worked at the operations centre of the VJ General Staff; is that correct? For the 2nd Army, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you understood that well, or maybe you misstated it. I wasn't working at the operations centre. I was working at the operations administration, it was called the first administration, that dealt with organising the units of the General Staff. Maybe it's not a good comparison, but like Registry is an organisational unit of the Tribunal; in the same way our operations administration was an organisational unit of the General Staff, and I was working in this first administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I misspoke, sir, I meant operations administration, not operations centre. Now we see -- you see the document on the screen before us is a document dated 1st April 1999, and it is sent from the Supreme Command Staff operations administration to the command of the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down on both versions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see it says there: "Written by: Colonel Kosta Novakovic." That would be you, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that this was signed by General Ojdanic, so it was prepared by you for General Ojdanic's signature?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see - if we could scroll up a bit in the English - we see that this order refers to the resubordination of the 37th Motorised Brigade to the command of the Pristina Corps 3rd Army. And it says that the resubordination will take place on 2nd April, 1999, by marching on the axis Raska-Kosovska Mitrovica-Srbica. Do you see that? That's number 2 that I'm reading out.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This unit that the -- this order refers to was based in the Raska area; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And pursuant to this order, it was deployed to Kosovo and subordinated to the Pristina Corps command on that date, on 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that this unit remained in Kosovo throughout the 1999 conflict, that is, all the way up to June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the commander of this unit, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's one of the lieutenant-colonels, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, before this order was issued by General Ojdanic to subordinate this unit to the Pristina Corps command, elements of this brigade were already in Kosovo, no, they had already been brought in to Kosovo by the commander of the 3rd Army. Do you recall that happening, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I can see from this order that the commander was already there. And it's my judgement that he was there to inspect his brigade and to conduct the so-called commander reconnaissance. But while we are at this order we should really note the date because it's important. The aggression was well under way, the Kosovo Verification Mission was no longer there, and there was no reason for this unit not to go into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not asking about that. I was just asking about the time when elements of this brigade came in, and we see that it's being deployed to the Srbica area, correct, that's what we see in number 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, but the date is very important. Otherwise I agree with you on all the other elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01530.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we get the same document back, P1530, and then we'll start from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Novakovic, my learned friend asserted based on this order that parts of this brigade had already been stationed in Kosovo and Metohija on the 1st of April when the order was issued. Can we establish that really based on this order?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Madam Prosecutor probably interpreted this para 3, where it says that the commander of the brigade shall accommodate the brigade, the commander who is in the sector. It's important to note the date, the 1st of April, whereas the bombing of the FRY - which we called NATO aggression, and in fact it was NATO aggression - started back on the 23rd of March. The bombardment was underway, and this commander had to go with his scouts to the area before his unit so that his unit would not be destroyed by the bombing. That's why he was there earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And item 1 says resubordinate the 37th Motorised Brigade. Does it mean the entire brigade?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then it says in item 2: "Carry out the resubordination by marching ..." Does it mean that the unit mentioned in item 1 should be marched in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says Raska-Kosovska Mitrovica-Srbica. I don't know if it was to be taken over solely by the march or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P01529.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But before we see it, after all these October Agreements did there occur a withdrawal of the army and all the other security forces into barracks out of Kosovo and Metohija as envisaged by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I kept emphasising that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not spend any more time on it. I have more questions. What about this area from which the security forces of Yugoslavia and Serbia withdrew, do you know what happened with that area from the withdrawal until the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The KLA, the terrorist forces, recovered that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it in keeping with the agreement signed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My learned friend pointed out this passage to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just go to the left in B/C/S. I can't see the date. On -- I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A reinforced unit carried out a tactical exercise on the topic of securing roads and capturing assigned facilities on the Pristina-Luzane village axis, general Podujevo sector. Can we see from this where this column was?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing this out. They went along the axis --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't noticed this straight away. Maybe -- may I continue now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let us wait for the Trial Chamber and their indication when you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to repeat that previous answer, Mr. Djurdjic, as it was missed all together in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, do you remember your previous answer, or shall I repeat my question? From what we just read that on 22nd [as interpreted] January the reinforced unit, the 15th Armoured Brigade, made up of 11 combat vehicles and 69 men, carried out a tactical exercise, et cetera, et cetera. Do we see how strong the unit was, where they went, and how long the tactical exercise lasted?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I had omitted an important element, because there is a highlighted passage here, and I don't read it -- I can't read it very well. But now I can see. This unit from 14 -- from 0800 to 1400 hours, so it's a very limited time-span, was on this assignment on the axis of Pristina-Luzane village, and that's the general Podujevo sector. From this we can conclude that the unit set off from Pristina towards Podujevo and returned within this time-span because it's very limited, from 0800 hours to 1400 hours. This follows logically from this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we now see P966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, I'd note that page 20, line 7, you are recorded as reading the 22nd of January, it was the 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't see the date at all. Something is highlighted. I said 20-something January. May I continue, Your Honour? Thank you. If we see on the screen P966, I'd like to request the page in B/C/S 14 I think -- no, 15, and it's 14 in English. Now I made a mistake. We need 14 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, my colleague read this out to you and then you moved to the next page, and that's where the question by Mrs. Kravetz ended. What is written below on this page, the second paragraph from the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to see the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no other exercises in this period. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So after the report by the operations duty officer, the conclusion is to be found in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were no other exercises in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But I can't see that we got it in English.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's there. Thank you. Mr. Novakovic, did the agreements that were signed ban any exercises in training in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, they were allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about this training centre, Batlava, did it exist even before these events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we called it a training-ground, and it was the best in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P837, page -- page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, my learned friend, Mrs. Kravetz, pointed out to you points 2, 4, and 5 of the agreement. I'd like to know whether these points, 2, 4, and 5 - and please look at point 7 as well - tell us whether our obligations under this agreement had been honoured by this time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said so many times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but who received reports at that time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Kosovo Diplomatic Mission, KDOM, that consisted of representatives of embassies, attaches and their assistants, a large number of officers in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at item 8 very carefully. It says: "With a view to verification of the implementation of these provisions, commanding officers of the Yugoslav Army and MUP shall report weekly -- will provide to KDOM/OSCE detailed weekly reports of manning, weapons, and activities of their forces." What does it mean "weekly"?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that even before the Kosovo Verification Mission started their work, KDOM, and through them the OSCE, had all the information about manning, weapons, and activities. And as we know, after the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived the KDOM was supposed to integrate with them. And upon its arrival the KVM had all the information about personnel, weapons, and activities, and these things that Drewienkiewicz asked for were already in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But when it says "weekly reports," what kind of activities can be covered by such a report?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it specifies very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm asking. Does it mean past circumstances or future circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, past.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Weekly, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a week for the past week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't think I need to show you again the Resolution 1199 concerning the relationship between KDOM and the KVM under that resolution. I'd only like one more thing, P967, please. It's a collegium meeting of the 3rd December 1998. Page 21 in B/C/S and 19 in English. It's a collegium of the Chief of the General Staff. We're interested in the contribution by Lieutenant-General Obradovic. It's another thing that had been covered by Mrs. Kravetz. No, the next page, please -- yeah, that's it, that's it. Milorad Obradovic. Do you see -- it's somewhere in the middle. We need to -- we need to draft a brief on the Vienna Agreement by 15 December, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What kind of Vienna Agreement is that and what was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vienna Agreement relates to the control of heavy weaponry, 12.7 millimetres and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What kind of legal document is it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the agreement on the subregional control of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic, for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and the assistance you have given. You may of course now return to your normal activities. A Court Officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are told, Mr. Djordjevic, that your witness is coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To repeat, good morning, since my microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us your full first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Vlajkovic, retired army colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of February, 1948, in the village of Omoljica, the municipality of Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide a statement to Mr. Ratko Djukanovic on the 17th of August, 2007, as well as an additional statement to Tomislav Visnjic on the 17th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you read both of them, and did you study them in detail before your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you state the same answers if asked the same things today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, but please bear in mind that I made a correction to paragraph 14 of the statement. I made it more precise and clear, and as far as I know, that is on the record. In terms of precision, I wanted to state what the mail procedure was used by the assistants in the Main Staff and the Supreme Command when they submitted such mail to the chief for signature. That was the description I provided, and I believe it is on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Chamber to admit both statements into evidence. The first one of the 17th of August, 2007, is D010-0697, and the other one of the 17th of September, 2007, is D010-711 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or 0711.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement D010-0697 will be Exhibit D00600 and the statement D010-0711 will be Exhibit D00601.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Milutinovic et al. case on the 20th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you provide the same answers as then, or would you change anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not. Perhaps I would expand on my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This transcript marked as D010-3937 is something that I seek to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00602.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness will testify today about the following. In the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999, the witness held the function of the chef de cabinet, Chief of the General Staff, as it was called during peacetime; or the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command during the NATO aggression. The witness will testify about his duties and obligations he had as the chef de cabinet of both the General Staff in peacetime as well as of the Supreme Command in war time. He will testify about how the cabinet, in keeping with annual and periodical work-plans and in co-operation with other organisational units, drafted work-plans for the Chief of Staff of the General Staff and the staff of the Supreme Command. He monitored the implementation of those plans. Changes to those plans could be undertaken without changing the gist of such plans only in emergency conditions or upon the request of the president of the FRY and the Supreme Council of Defence or by intervention of superior institutions. The cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff in peacetime or the staff of the -- Supreme Command Staff in war time and the chief of cabinet, in keeping with its function, regularly participated and co-operated with the operational administration for operational staff in the preparation of the agendas for regular meetings and briefings held by the Chief of the General Staff and the Supreme Command Staff, which he had to verify in advance. The witness provided the technical aspects such as the making of audio and visual recordings. He also wants to point out at the -- point out the mistakes which may have occurred during such meetings that were of technical nature. He will also testify about the meetings and documentation created in the wake of such meetings. He will also explain how he prepared mail which required the signature of the Chief of Staff or the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and how it was archived. The witness will also comment on different documents explaining what a reception stamp is, as well as the Registry log number or what errors could be made or what notations could be made by the Chief of the General Staff on such documents themselves. The documents have been kept in the log-books under the dates they were received. Mistakes could occur in terms of entering the correct date. As the chief of cabinet, he had no knowledge of any member of the Supreme Command Staff ordering or approving any type of activities which would be contrary to international humanitarian law in terms of committing war crimes. Quite to the contrary, the witness will confirm that numerous documents strictly prohibited such conduct. He will also testify that during NATO aggression he has the chef de cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff was with the chief of the Supreme Command Staff at the command post on a daily basis. He attended daily briefings and situation analyses. Due to the virtue of his function, the witness attended briefings given to the Chief of the General Staff, and pursuant to his orders he precisely defined tasks in linguistic terms and subsequently distributed them to those who were in charge of implementing them. He also followed the implementation of those tasks and submitted reports on the same. The witness will testify about who was in attendance at those meetings. He will also explain that he has no knowledge of any ethnic cleansing operations in Kosovo and Metohija as operations which had been planned at the end of 1998. He will explain that at the meetings of the Supreme Command Staff and during the briefings, there were no informations of any war crimes committed until early June 1999. The witness will testify that operations of the Army of Yugoslavia in their defence of the territory against the KLA and a possible attack by NATO were never directed against the Albanian population with the aim of driving them out. The increase of forces in 1999 was primarily focused on the defence of the country from the KLA and NATO. This is the summary of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, first I'll have a number of general questions to put to you, and then we'll move to certain documents and I will require your comment upon those. Given that we speak the same language, I must ask you that following my questions you pause shortly so that the interpreters would be able to interpret for all those in the courtroom what I had said. Please answer only following that pause, and I of course also need to bear in mind to do the same once you have completed your answers. Let us begin. Colonel, what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Following the elementary school, I completed the military high school, natural sciences, in Belgrade. After that, the land forces academy, specialisation in artillery. In 1971 I became an artillery lieutenant. Between 1980 and 1982 I completed the military political higher school at the level of staff, which is a precondition to receive the rank of a colonel. Between 1987 and 1990 I received my master's degree in military science, specialisation in political matters. There were no particular other courses that I undertook, save for a number of courses I attended outside the regular schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now in the form of a narrative tell us about your career.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: From the time I graduated from the military academy and receiving the rank of second lieutenant, I was commander of platoon for three years, for two years I was battery commander, then for two years I was assistant for moral guidance in an artillery battalion. For two years after that I was chief of a class of the higher military school, artillery section. After that I was head of class of the military academy, again artillery section. For 18 months I was assistant for moral guidance in a school for active-duty officers. In 1985, in December, I was transferred, or rather, applied for the post and obtained the post of lecturer in a high military school, and that's where I stayed until 1990. In the meantime I received my master's degree. In 1991 I was moved to the administration for information and moral guidance of the General Staff, and in 1994 I was appointed to the office of the Chief of the General Staff as deputy chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff. In 2000 I was sent for preparations to become military attache in Vienna, and that's what I did from 2001 until 2005, when upon meeting all the requirements in terms of age and years of service I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that you retired quite regularly?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I fulfilled all the legal conditions for retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I now ask you to explain what your duties were in 1998 when this institution where you worked was still called General Staff and you were the chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe to the best of your ability your work there, your job description, your duties and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The responsibilities of the office of the Chief of the General Staff are rather precisely defined in the instruction on the competencies of the organisational units of the General Staff. According to those instructions, the office was to provide all the material, technical and other support, to the Chief of the General Staff and the deputy Chief of the General Staff. The office also had to take care that the tasks of the General Staff are implemented to prepare work-plans, to prepare and distribute mail that was presented to the General Staff chief for his information and signature. And the office also processed other mail that did not have to pass by the desk of the Chief of the General Staff. He only had to be told that it was of such and such a nature and that it had been taken care of. The office also dealt with the security of the General Staff and the chief. We took security measures, both at the office and during travel. The office had on its staff personnel who were qualified and responsible for dealing with staffing issues, financial issues, and something that is included in what I said first, providing all the possible support to the General Staff and its chief in the realisation of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned security measures at the office and during travel. Can you tell us briefly what security measures were in effect at the office itself, not -- not those that were directed at persons, but security measures in dealing with mail, with written documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff has a security unit, and through this security unit the office of the General Staff also made sure that all the mail and all the parcels went through a security check. We called it - and it is in essence - the procedure of anti-sabotage control. These security checks were done at the forwarding unit of the General Staff which would affix an appropriate stamp once the security check was completed, and without that stamp we did not present anything to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So it was called anti-sabotage control, BDK?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Which unit at the office of the Chief of the General Staff, later called Supreme Command Staff, dealt with anti-sabotage control?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the forwarding unit where all the mail comes in, and it was conducted under the supervision of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back later to that topic. My next question is: Did you have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to our establishment there was an establishment post of deputy chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff and a deputy chief of office for the deputy Chief of the General Staff. So this deputy chief was a connection between me and the deputy Chief of the General Staff. The deputy who worked on all these issues with me was Colonel Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: First name?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Radoicic. It was in the nature of our work to share everything with him so that in my absence he could stand in for me and so that work should run smoothly, even in my absence. As for obligations and responsibilities, it was very difficult to distinguish between the two of us because we both did everything, except that he was familiar with all the tasks to such a level that enabled him to take over when I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, if I understood correctly, practically did the same work that you did except that he was not the chief responsible?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, practically all that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think before I move to my next set of questions this is a good time for a break, 10.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we will continue. Can you please tell us what the annual and periodical and monthly work-plans are that came from the office of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff primarily implemented his duties in accordance with those plans. We drafted the plans as monthly and annual plans. We developed them in accordance with the annual and monthly plans of the General Staff. We placed all the duties of the chief into the plan in relation to superiors, to subordinates, according to the elements of each of his activities. The plan of the Chief of the General Staff was something that the Chief of the General Staff adhered to. There were certain deviations in terms of changes because of the president, the Supreme Defence Council, and the General Staff. But primarily, this was a document to which the chief stuck to a great degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: What was the position or the attitude of the office towards the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Supreme Defence Council and the federal government, the position of the chief of the Supreme Command? And by that I'm thinking of their personal relations, correspondence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief -- the office of the Chief of the General Staff had excellent co-operation with the military cabinet of the president of the republic or the president of the Supreme Defence Council and the communication between us and the president proceeded exclusively through the office. The chief of the office was General Slavoljub Susic. And while working with him in the distribution of documents and co-ordination of certain activities, there were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what the collegium sessions are of the Supreme Command Staff or the General Staff in peacetime. Did you prepare for such sessions? Was that part of your duties? Could you clarify that as much as you are able to, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the work-plans, the collegium was a body that had regular meetings. In peacetime these were sessions of the collegium of the General Staff, and in the technical sense decisions by the General Staff were finalised in the collegium. The agenda of the collegium was prepared by the organisational units of the General Staff. The office of the chief had as its duty, pursuant to the agenda of the collegium which was drafted in consultation with other organisational units of the General Staff, to present that to the chief; after which he would verify it. And then this agenda would serve as the basis for the preparation of documents and other technical aspects of that meeting. There were presentations, slides, documents that were needed and had to be prepared previously for these meetings. So that was the duty of the office. So based on an agenda which was approved by the chief, all the documents and necessary things for the meetings were prepared. The preparations for the collegium sessions - and now I'm talking about the peacetime sessions - we would organise the audio recording of these sessions. And then after the audio recording a transcript would be made, and those transcripts would be archived and registered in the log-book of the office. Each collegium session was accompanied by some technical and professional aspects that were in our care. For example, when there would be a coffee break or a refreshment break, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about war time and sessions of the collegium or sessions of the Supreme Command Staff, the official name of such meetings was briefings or reports to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. But since we transferred to this war time formation overnight, just pure by inertia -- just purely by inertia, sometimes we would call it briefing, sometimes collegium, sometimes evening meetings, but this was such a form of work where the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and his subordinates would report on certain matters from their area of work. And I would like to note that during war time, during briefings, in the Supreme Command Staff these briefings were not recorded and the minutes from those meetings were kept in a special book which was done by the operations administrations in the Supreme Command. Two colonels were entrusted with these duties, to monitor the addresses, the commands, the speeches, and then to note that down and to verify that in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to digress slightly here, but I think this is essential at this point. Can you please tell me the General Staff in peacetime and the Supreme Command Staff in war time, are you able to make some kind of comparison in their work once this peacetime institution transformed into a war time institution? I think you are competent to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the command and control system, the position of the collegium or the place of reporting, actually, is not something that is very different --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you here. What we're interested at this point is for you to make a distinction between the office of the General Staff -- I'm not talking about the collegiums or briefings now. I'm talking about the duties of the Supreme Command Staff office. Can you make a comparison between these two periods of operation, or would the difference only be in the name?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The difference in the name came about from the changed volume of duties. The General Staff in peacetime was primarily engaged with subordinate units and directed its activities in that area; in war time this would be the Supreme Command Staff, and its work became more complex. It grew, the number of tasks and assignments became greater. So in that sense the staff had more duties and had more work, and even though it was operating at a different location and had a smaller staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can go back now to the topic that we were on previously. Who actually comprised the collegium? Or let me ask you this: Who attended the meetings of the Supreme Command Staff during war time? Was that some kind of regular meeting, or was it something that would be subject to change?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The composition of the office was -- actually the assistants of the Chief of General Staff, these would be heads of sectors and heads of independent administrations. This would be the permanent composition. Depending on the agenda, the collegium could be attended by other officers too. I'm talking about senior officers. If the question of borders was discussed, then the meeting would be attended by the chief of the section from the operations administration in charge of that particular area. The collegium had expanded meetings from time to time which were attended by the commanders of the strategic groupations [as interpreted, the commands of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Armies, the air force, navy, and anti-aircraft and special unit commanders, so these units which were directly subordinated to the General Staff. There was situations when the chief, because it was necessary to react quickly, would summon only some of his assistants in order to deal with a particular problem. We would call that the inner collegium. This was something when it was not essential for all the others to participate in, and it was when urgent or very specific questions were being dealt with. So we have the permanent composition, the expanded or broader composition, and sometimes we have the inner collegium. If necessary, I can also comment that from the point of view of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is most important to us.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: These briefings which are practically the same as the collegium were also attended by the assistants of the General Staff, the independent administration. And depending on the matters being considered, someone from other organisational units of the General Staff could also attend in order to clarify specific professional matters. Depending on the tactical bearer of a particular assignment, the chief of that particular section would attend and he would explain the topic or the matter being discussed. During the bombing or the aggression, the briefings at one point were not attended by any other persons who were not members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am first of all interested in 1998 when we're talking about the office of the Chief of the General Staff, and then later could you please draw a parallel with the body when it was the office of the chief of the Supreme Command. Could you tell me if you yourself took part by establishment in these collegiums. By the nature of your position did you attend the evening briefings, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the duties that I had in preparing for the collegiums and the briefings and because of the work I had after that or during the collegium sessions and afterwards, I attended all of those meetings. Sometimes for justified reasons if I was not there, if I was unable to attend, my deputy would attend who was familiar with all aspects of the work. But this would only happen in situations when I would not be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the gentleman you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Colonel Milan Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As chief of the office of the Supreme Command Staff, did you monitor the implementation of assignments or directives that you received by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command relating to the collegiums and the briefings, the daily briefings; and if so, who did you report back to, what was your reporting duty in terms of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff particularly insisted that upon completion of collegium sessions or briefings, assignments that he would issue during such meetings be formulated precisely during the summing-up, for example. So while we were consulting, if necessary, with the relevant administrations or by looking at the minutes at the Supreme Command Staff, we would formulate the -- these things and process them and distribute them to those who would be responsible for their implementation. This would be done after the collegium sessions by the end of the workday. And in the Supreme Command Staff staff after the briefings we would complete that by the end of the day or by midnight at the latest. So these assignments would be received by those responsible for carrying them out by the time the meeting was over. My task was to follow and monitor the implementation of these assignments, and then at the next meeting or briefing it was my duty to refer -- report to the chief and everyone present about the degree to which the tasks were implemented. The chief insisted on this, and we adhered to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These documents that you drafted after these meetings, the collegium sessions and later during the war after the evening briefings, were then sent to the institutions they were addressed to, to the commands, the administrations, the sectors. What I'm interested in is in the technical aspect. How was this logged in the cabinet? If something was dispatched from the cabinet, was it somebody's duty to log that; and if so, how was it done, what was the manner in which it was done, and who was it done by?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The data was processed and logged in the log-book of the office, which implies that the document was stamped, there was a date placed, there was a stamp placed on the document register, and then one copy would be registered and then archived at the office of the -- at the archive of the cabinet. All of the documents bear their number, certification, and stamp, and the addressee; and they were dispatched to all those who had certain duties and who were issued with certain assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: These documents, were they sorted according to some other criteria? For example, according to the classification or something else.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: All the assignments at the collegium were of a confidential nature, and that is how they were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That means that access in the technical sense -- actually, it means that the document could only be dispatched to the person it was addressed to. A copy had to be saved in the archives, and the recipient of the document had to treat the document as a confidential one, meaning that they had to log that document also and stamp it in order to confirm this, which would indicate that the document was received and registered in the log-book, and as such, archived in the vault and kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the technical aspect of this document that would be dispatched from your cabinet. Were you obliged to enter some other markings, for example, the number of copies of a certain document or anything that would be relevant that you could tell us now relating to this technical aspect of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Other than the elements laid down in the rules, we did not make any other markings or any other technical elements. As I said, in the section that -- where the document -- to whom the document would be dispatched, this would be recorded. But since it was not strictly confidential, we did not have the duty to place numbers on each of the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But all the documents leaving the office were confidential. Some of them were perhaps strictly confidential. Would they be treated differently if we're talking about strictly confidential documents? Were there any other classifications which were used pursuant to the rules that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, documents can be state or military secret, then they can be confidential, strictly confidential, or for internal use only. State documents are always strictly confidential. Military documents could receive different grades, such as military secret, confidential, strictly confidential, or internal use only. Military documents that were strictly confidential, technically speaking, were processed in such a way that each document would receive a copy number, that is to say copy number 1, 2, 3, or 4 following the list of distribution. If it is copy number 3 sent, say, to the command of the 3rd Army, then we knew that that particular copy belonged to them alone. If it bore the number 2, it could not be sent to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the dispatching of these documents given the degree of confidentiality, as you have explained as being part of the rules, what was the handling treatment in terms of distributing those documents to the end user, to the addressees themselves? How was that forwarded?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the degree of confidentiality and urgency, that is how they were distributed. Each document would be placed in an envelope bearing the same Registry number as well as the sign of degree of confidentiality. You would know based on the envelope what the type of the document is. If it was strictly confidential, it was treated as such, in the sense of registering it, keeping track of it, archiving it, distributing it, and so on and so forth. If a document was urgent, the envelope would bear that sign. It would be a signal to us to take it to the Chief of the General Staff or of the Supreme Command Staff for signature. We knew if we had to do that immediately or if we could do that together with other mail, which happened twice a day. Anything that was urgent was sent to him immediately. We didn't allow ourselves, and we were not allowed by the chief to violate that rule. In case the chief was absent, under his authority it could be done by his deputy, to open such an urgent document and follow it up. I hope this is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the way documents were dispatched depending on the categories you have enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Urgent documents could be sent by telegram or by courier, also depending on our assessment. Strictly confidential documents bearing that sign would be sent to the forwarding -- mail forwarding room by courier, inside a courier bag that was locked. It would be opened in the mail room and forwarded depending on the degree of confidentiality. The courier in the process of bringing it or taking out mail was unable to open his bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall a letter of Ms. Louise Arbour of the 29th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I do. If I may add something, I can tell you that my memory was jogged during the Milutinovic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that letter subsequently, and we'll show it to you. My next question is this: There is something you said in paragraph 19 of your statement. Is it true when you say that you were with the chief of the Supreme Command Staff at the command post all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the command post all the time, which doesn't necessarily mean that we shared the same office all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: During the aggression, what did that mean for you when you spent your time at the command post, and the same goes for the gentleman who replaced you occasionally?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: We were forced to spend the whole day there. We were resolving issues, creating conditions for the work of the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff which required a dynamic approach and day-long engagement. In order to be able to cope with that tempo, I organised shifts in the office. If I was resting, my deputy was there. Other services in the office were also organised in such a way that they could react immediately to any request of the chief of Supreme Command Staff. The number of tasks multiplied, and he began asking for more detailed and precise information and reaction to any particular document. And I hope by having organised us the way we did, we managed to meet his requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you did not go home during the aggression, or can that be explained in some other way because you say you were there all day long?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I went home, let's say, once a week for two to three hours, to take a shower, change clothes, and go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about your deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you co-operate with the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, did the chief of Supreme Command Staff have any contact with the MUP during the aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were official contacts, but it never happened at the Supreme Command Staff. At the command post where we were, where the Supreme Command Staff was deployed, there was no one else save for military personnel with special permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm particularly interested in knowing whether you knew the accused, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, personally who was then head of security of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think when Minister Stojiljkovic visited once the Chief of the General Staff, he was escorted by Mr. Djordjevic. Otherwise, I had no further contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about 1999 and the time of aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
