utterances.text: As the chief of office of the chief of Supreme Command Staff during the aggression, did you have any communication with the Ministry of the Interior or the public security sector head in the sense that you received correspondence from them or you sent documents to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no official communication between the office and the minister's office of the Ministry of the Interior, including Mr. Djordjevic. I don't see -- I don't remember a single document that was either sent to or received from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for the answers so far. I would like to clarify a different matter now, and I believe you are the relevant person to put those questions to. What is the source of the documents for which we can say -- you said you testified in the Milutinovic et al. case. On that occasion you saw different military documents. Can you tell us something about the source of those documents, if you recall that period; if not, I'll show you different documents and then put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the aggression stopped under the authority of the chief of Supreme Command Staff or the Chief of General Staff in peacetime all war time material had to be archived and handed over to the military archives. As far as I know, in late 1999 and in 2000 that was indeed done. This meant that all documents pertaining to war time activities were transferred to the military archives. Taking documents out of the military archives could only happen if there was an order or a permission given by the custodian, that is to say the archives. Officially speaking, one could not receive archive documents by any other channels except from the archives themselves following their approval. If documents were lent by the archives and copied, they received appropriate stamps. If a document bears the stamp of the military archives, then it means that it was actually deposited in the archives and kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any documents in your previous testimony which did not originate from the military archives; if so, how could you explain the nature of such documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw certain documents which do not bear the stamp of the military archive. It is possible that these documents were received even before their transfer to the archives or by other means. There may have been copies made before the documents were transferred or they may come from the bulk of documents of a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Chamber to allow us to use the usher when we intend to show documents to the witness, for the usher to hand over the binder with the hard copies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1243 put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 1. We'll wait for the document to appear, in B/C/S as well. Do we have it in B/C/S? This is the translation. Could we please zoom in a bit. That's good. Mr. Vlajkovic, what kind of a document is this? Can you give us a detailed description in relation to what you have said so far, and of course from the point of view of your duty as the chief of office of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a rule pertaining to official correspondence and office administration in the Army of Yugoslavia from 1994, that is to say the rule in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does it entail?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It uniformly regulates the handling of military documents. In detail the rule explains and regulates the handling of documents as of the moment of their creation until the moment of archiving. This means technical processing, the format, the degree of secrecy and confidentiality, use, registering, forwarding, receiving, photocopying or multiplication, signing, et cetera. In the part pertaining to office administration, it elaborates the handling of documents as of the moment of receiving in the mailroom, the opening of such documents, registering, sorting, processing, submitting for signature, et cetera. The title of the rule is: Rule on official correspondence and office administration in the Army of Yugoslavia, meaning that all units of the Army of Yugoslavia had to handle their documents in the way prescribed and to treat it in the spirit of this regulation. This is how we can tell whether a document was properly technically processed, whether it was handled properly -- appropriately, and whether there is anything wrong with it. The rule is quite precise, particularly when it comes to preservation, archiving, and distribution of documents. We followed the rule in the office, which makes it easier for us to recognise such documents where the procedure was not followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now confirm that this rule is, in fact, what you called earlier in your evidence the rule book and the instruction on office management, is this the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any other rule book or any other instruction regarding office management?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This one nullifies all the previous ones, and this is the one that was in force when I was working, during my tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: 1998/1999, the time when I served at the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is already exhibited, I believe, Your Honours. Can I now call up D010-074.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it's D010-0719.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's 2. Now we have both on the monitors. You spoke about the way you worked and what your obligations were. You described this in detail in your evidence earlier and today. I want to ask you: What is this that we're looking at, best of all, is it an authentic document from your office; and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the format, the technical features and the contents, it's a document created at the office. I am the author, as you can see from the signature. And it is usual communication of the sort I exchanged with assistants, chiefs of the General Staff, both in peacetime and in war time. So when the Chief of the General Staff notes on the margins of the document or gives me a verbal order, I formulate into a document; and as such, it is attached to the document and submitted to the chief of the operations department and to the deputy chief of the Supreme Command Staff, including tasks ordered by the Chief of the General Staff and just formulated by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you would formulate the chief's instructions on a separate piece of paper, it is the result of an order that you received, or can you describe this in detail?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we give a certain document to the chief along with our suggestions, if we have any, he reviews it and he can either write on the margins what needs to be done -- we used to call that annotations on the document. He would write in his own hand what to do concerning that document or to whom to copy it. I would take that down in my copy book, and then I would write it up on a separate piece of paper. I thought that the assistant needed to receive a clean copy reflecting the annotations of the chief. This concerns a letter of the then-chief Prosecutor of the ICTY, Louise Arbour, addressed to the Chief of the General Staff and the commander of the 3rd Army. And we presented this to the chief. The chief ordered us to prepare a draft order to prevent the commission of war crimes, as Mrs. Louise Arbour asked. So in this case what did the chief ask us to do? He asked us to prepare a draft order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Stop here. You need to explain. You said officers Marjanovic and Kovacevic, who are they by establishment?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: General Marjanovic was deputy chief of the Supreme Command Staff, and General Blagoje Kovacevic was assistant for operations and staff affairs. The chief ordered us to prepare a draft order. When the responsible administration submitted this through me for signature, the chief looked at it and said, "Give it to Marjanovic and Kovacevic to review it and to make corrections, if any."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby tender this for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00603.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you to look at another document, D010-0721. That's your tab 3. Okay, now it's legible. Again we see this separate sheet, as you called it. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When Generals Marjanovic and Kovacevic and the assistant -- that is, assistant of the Chief of the General Staff and chief of the operations sector reviewed the draft order and made the suggestions, I was required to return the draft order to the author with this cover letter, asking them to include the suggestions and corrections into the order. So this cover letter and the original draft order were returned by me to the department that was responsible for drafting, in connection with the letter by Louise Arbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00604.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up D217.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's tab 4. Can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order -- the order we discussed regarding those two separate sheets. It's the final version signed by the chief, and it was drafted including the modifications made by the generals I mentioned. And as such, it was distributed to various units mentioned on the last page. So that's the order signed by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and sent down to the units. It concerns the prevention of war crimes in the spirit of the letter by Mrs. Arbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Look at this. You saw the first page as well. Was this the usual procedure -- because you explained the contents already. Was this the usual procedure when following the orders of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was created in complete accordance with the prescribed procedure and delivered to the units listed here. All these units were subordinated to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. One noteworthy thing is that this document was received from the military archive because it bears their stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The technical processing indicates that its authentic. All the technical indicators confirm it, and the seal of the military archive confirms it was received from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been exhibited. The next document will be D010-0742.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's tab 5. Please look at it. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This document was created at the office of the Chief of the General Staff. On the orders of the Chief of the General Staff I created a document addressed to all the units indicated by the chief and requiring them to provide the office with all the documents they had produced so far in connection with the prevention of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law. This document is directly linked to the previous order. The chief first gave an order and then requires feedback what -- about what was done to execute that order, except that he extends his requirement to the period before the order. You can see on the second page to whom it was delivered. All these units were required to submit all the documents for the period before the aggression and after the 24th of March concerning the prevention of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law. You can see the addressees on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the organisational units were required to make available to the office --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on this passage on the left as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You signed this?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the left I just want to see this without the signature. That is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00605.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is tab 6, and I'd like to call up D008-2472.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a new document. It says: "Reporting to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff or a briefing." The format doesn't matter. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably a transcript of the minutes from a briefing. Minutes were kept in an A4 copy book, and somebody transcribed these minutes. I don't see that the transcript is verified or authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: We can't see any authorisation of this transcript. There's no indication that it's been verified. And as far as the substance is concerned we can see certain deficiencies that make it difficult to decide what it really is, certain imprecisions that combined with the lack of any data about verification make it difficult to determine how authentic it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00606.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up D008-2190.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In you're binder it's tab 7, Colonel. Here we see a document under the same title, different date. It says: "Attended by 17 persons." Tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's again a transcript from the book of minutes kept at briefings of the Supreme Command Staff. This one is of the 7th of April. It has the same features as the previous one, unauthorised with many imprecisions that make it difficult to interpret it. On page 3 here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you go on I've been holding Ms. Kravetz for some time. She has an objection -- oh, the moment has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't notice, Your Honour, either. We can see page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 we have somewhere in the fourth paragraph my name, Colonel Vlajkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but we do not have an equivalent page in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'm wondering what is the case now. It should be also third page. Wait a minute. Next page in English. No. There is no interpretation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the very first page of this document, it seems we may not have the correct document at all as the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, it seems that it is on the first page in English and third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the two documents appear to be quite different on looking at the screens, the format -- if you look at the length of paragraph 2 in Serbian, it's long; and short in English. Whereas, in Serbian paragraph 3 is short, but it's long in English. Quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have in my docs translation in English but in hard copy, and this document is marked with D008-2194. But it seems that it is not right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you look at the date and the times at the top --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but one is a meeting from 1800 until 1930. The other is a meeting from 2030 or 2100 to 2215, two different times on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on the next document. [Interpretation] We're not going to ask that this document to be admitted. Evidently there has been some confusion here, but the Defence just wanted to confirm with this document what we heard earlier. The next document is D568. Can we please look at that on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder this is tab 8, sir, and we see it here on the screen. Can we please have your comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time during my testimony here at the Tribunal. This is a document that was compiled at the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in October 2001, when I was no longer at the office at my previous post. The document was compiled in violation of the rules and regulations regulating the drafting and archiving of documents in the military, in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: From the technical aspect, the format does not correspond, and you cannot see a summary like this anywhere. I really don't know why this summary was compiled in the first place. This is a non-standard format, an overview, and only the person who actually made this overview knows why they did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know perhaps who requested this summary to be made?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Evidently the summary originated from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia or from the Chief of the General Staff from the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I have to interrupt you here.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the Chief of the General Staff was Colonel Pavkovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue. The year?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The document was compiled in 2001, and it's an overview of the archive's materials from 1998 and 1999. I have previously said that by an order of the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, all the archived materials from the war had to be archived by the end of 1999, which means that this is some other type of archiving of those documents not based on the rules and regulations of archiving in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the answer you gave previously, you said that Mr. -- or actually, General Dragoljub Ojdanic ordered that all the documents should be archived by the end of 1999. Was this done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to what I know this was done. As far as archived materials from the office, since I was certain -- it was certain already that I was leaving the office, I handed this task to my deputy, Colonel Milan Radoicic. And in -- he technically processed all the materials and documents dating from that period, and through the office with the accompanying documents that are sent with the archive materials list which I saw later, he submitted the complete set to the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia. This means that all the documents from the period of the war were archived at the military archives, all the documents originating or from the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This will be -- actually, can we look at documents D585 and P888. Can we look at these documents both at the same time. This would be tabs 9 and 10 in the binder, so we're looking at D585 and P888, please. I asked for both documents to be shown in English side by side. We're looking at the documents in B/C/S. I was asking for the English versions of D585 and P888, if we can look at the English versions of the documents, please. I'm doing this in order to assist the Trial Chamber and my friends from the Prosecution. Can we look at the next page, please. The following page of each of the documents, please. Excellent. Thank you. And we can see from this that this is a document which on the face of it has the same content, but now let us look at the B/C/S versions of D585 and P888. Can we look at the first page of each of those documents and can we put them side by side, please. Can we look at the right-hand document. Can we make it a little bit smaller so that we can see the corners of the page. Thank you. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, you also have the hard copy in front of you. Can you please look at this document and can you tell me whether you recognise this document. Have you seen it before? We can see to whom the document is addressed.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time when I testified in the Milutinovic et al. case -- both documents actually. Up until that time, I did not see or register seeing this document at the office, neither by the format or content.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document on the first page of each of the documents, can you comment first of all on the adherence to the rules on office operation that we talked about a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the technical characteristics, these are two different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 248 is one marking, and then 94/1 is 1-2, which would indicate -- actually, it does not confirm that this would be a copy of the same document. The document on the left-hand has the stamp of the military archive, meaning that it was received from the military archive, this is document marked 248. The right-hand document marked with 72 does not have that same stamp which would indicate that it was received from a different source.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, can you tell me on the right-hand side of each of the documents we have the words "military secret, strictly confidential," and then we have copy number, and a line. You were talking about that a little bit earlier. So I would like to ask you if this perhaps indicates something else.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Documents marked "military secret, strictly confidential" had to be distributed with the copy of the document indicated. For example, a copy could be marked copy number 1, and then in the list you would have copy number 1 archived. And then number 2 sent to the Supreme Command Staff. And then at the bottom it would say that it was dispatched to the Supreme Command Staff. This number is not present here, so in that sense this document is not properly drafted or processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2 of each document, please. Can we place the document so that we can see the stamp and the signature at the bottom of each of the documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at page 2 of each of these documents and can you add anything else about them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The left document has the stamp of the military archive, meaning that the document was received from the military archives. There is no such stamp on the document on the right-hand side. Then as far as format is confirmed -- concerned, the document does not state to whom it was dispatched, because it can also be dispatched to other addressees, not just to the commander. It could be provided to somebody for purposes of information, but this would need to be stated. Then we see that the signature is evidently different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in onto the part on the right-hand side where it says "komandant," commander, where we can see the signature and the stamp so that we can see that more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We are looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not a handwriting analysis expert, but it's evident here that it's not the signature and the stamp is different, indicating that it's a different copy, not a copy of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the whole page of each of the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is in the bottom left-hand corner? Can we see? There is something in the left-hand bottom corner of the document, but we do not see that on the document on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The left document contains a stamp of the office of the Supreme Command Staff, which would lead us to conclude that the document was at the office and was logged in at the office. On the right-hand side, there is no such stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you presume what the source of the first document is and what the source of the second document is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The source of the first one is the military archives. I cannot tell you anything about the source of the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question concerning the document is this: You looked at the contents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If this document was indeed received by the Supreme Command Staff, what should have been done with it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once received by the office following the procedure I've already explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can skip that.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: -- it would be presented to the Chief of the General Staff. Judging by the contents, I -- it is difficult for me to believe that the chief would not react to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it required certain follow-up by different people. There was several tasks contained therein, both horizontally and vertically speaking in terms of hierarchy. This document could not have gone without the signature of the chief or without a separate note with tasks specified. When I look at the reception stamp it says "military secret, strictly confidential, personally for the chief of Supreme Command Staff," and the Registry number is questionable. Such an important document is not registered --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Are you talking about page number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see page 1 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand side corner it says 3rd Army command, strictly confidential, number so and so. The significance of the document and the person it was addressed to would not mean that it would be archived with only five or six numbers. In the log-book of the 3rd Army, it required a separate number because there would be other documents as the -- as a result of this one, and the numbers would start with 1 and go on up to 3 or 4. The number itself is rather problematic. To me it means that this was additionally added to a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Given your position and the significance of this document, could it have happened that you knew nothing whatsoever about this document and the documents which followed -- which were supposed to follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to believe that I would not have noticed it, either because of its significance or because of the documents that would be required as a follow-up and that were supposed to be issued by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be wiser even not to embark upon this right now because this set of questions, given the number of documents that I intend to show, is very important for the Defence, and I will conclude that in the next session. Therefore, it would be better to start this topic after the break, particularly it is very important for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in your binder it is tab 11, and I would kindly ask for P1240 to be put on the screen. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The document was created in the command of the Pristina Corps. It was sent to the 3rd Army command, to their forward command post. It serves to -- goes to confirm that this document was not within my reach. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see it before the previous case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of a person who was familiar with the procedure presented today, can you comment the technical aspects of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The document is strictly confidential. It's a military secret, but there is no file number and no copy number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That the procedure on office management was not followed. Then on page 2 -- sorry, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You need page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2 we don't have a distribution list. In this -- in that case we would have copy number 1, copy number 2, and so on. It is signed by the corps commander, and there is a Registry stamp of the 3rd Army command, meaning -- or which could mean, if the document is authentic, that it was received by that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you arrive at any other conclusion in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Registry numbers, given the significance of this document and the persons involved would have required long numbers with many digits, and it is not quite clear to me why it is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that contrary to the procedure we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, contrary to the regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please next move to P1505.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Mr. Vlajkovic, it is tab 12. We'll wait for the document to appear. Very well. Colonel, have you had occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a telegram of the command of the 3rd Army, also strictly confidential and urgent, sent to the sector of the staff of the Supreme Command, in particular land forces sector. It is a request to deal with certain problems that had to do with combat-readiness of the Pristina Corps. There was a possibility to have that forwarded directly to the sector for ... Although it says "urgent," it doesn't mention that it was supposed to be sent by telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What would be the usual way?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It would have said "urgent telegram."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What other technical aspects can you mention concerning office management?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: We don't see a single signature there, no signature of the commander, of Lieutenant-General Nebojsa Pavkovic, and no signature of the Chief of Staff, Mr. Stojimirovic, that the telegram could be sent. Thirdly, there is no stamp which would indicate that the telegram was technically processed or the document was sent as a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the rules would interpret that as a document that was not sent. Had it been sent, the person who was supposed to process it would have applied the stamp and have entered all the necessary details about the reception and dispatch of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the fact that it wasn't signed by Commander Nebojsa Pavkovic and that it was not signed by Chief of Staff, Major-General Ljubisa Stojimirovic? You just mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It means that the person who was supposed to send the telegram would not have been able to do that without their signatures -- or rather, was not supposed to do that. That would have been against the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you have learned of such a document had it ever arrived to the Supreme Command Staff, because it was one of the addressees?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily because it was sent to the land forces sector and they could have dealt with it within their own purview, or they could have reported to and consulted with the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. This would have been a perfectly legal way to go about it, to have the sector deal with it itself without going through the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please next have P584 [as interpreted] and D583, one next to each other at the same time on the screen if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder these would be tabs 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Ms. O'Leary draws my attention to a mistake in the transcript. I said D583 and D584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we're looking at that, the previous telegram, is that an exhibit? Could you give me the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I've already indicated that. It is P1505.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Here we have two archived lists in English. Could we please go to page 2 in both these documents, both please. The first document, the one on the left, we should have, I believe, page 7 with the entry number 82. Very good. Entry number 82. Next could we go to the last page in both documents, the very bottom of the page so as to be able to see the signature block. Very good. Next could we have the same two documents on the screen but in B/C/S, and it should be page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, as I've said already, in your binder you have hard copies of both documents in tabs 13 and 14. First tell me whether what you can see is familiar to you; and if so, tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, any archival tasks were handed over by me to my deputy, Colonel Radoicic, because I departed the office. In any case, I was privy to the process and procedure, and I am familiar with this document from that time as well as because of the previous case I testified in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now have a look at the document on the left side and on the right side. Having in mind your knowledge of the rules and the rule on business management in particular, please tell us what it is that you can observe on these documents. As we can see, they're both photocopies of some originals.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an archive list compiled in the office of the Chief of the General Staff, and served as the basis for the hand-over of war time material to the military archives of the VJ. It contains all those documents that were handed over to the military archives. The hand-over was conducted on the 10th of August, 1992. 277 documents were handed over, totalling 735 pages. The other copy that I have here is different from the first, because when it was being photocopied the column with the contents of documents was covered, and this one does not have a stamp of the military archives. On the one that has the stamp we see the description of all documents that were on the lists. When something is being archived in the military archives, a separate procedure is followed. There have to be three copies of each document bound together. The person working in the archives checks whether the document under number 1 contains three pages on two pieces of which paper. So that's what he does. He carries out that check and enters corrections if there were mistakes made, and I can explain what sort of mistakes those can be. At the end he adds up the figures as well as the number of corrections and the number of documents and number of pages. He enters the total in the upper right-hand corner because it is required by the format. It says here that 277 documents were handed over totalling 735 pages. This is something that can be easily checked. The person receiving archival material takes document number 1, for example. He establishes that these are actually two documents containing three pages. He crossed out the number 2 and entered the number 3, that is the number of pages. Sometimes we counted sheets and the archivist counted pages. Sometimes there can be some confusion about the cover and whether it is counted separately. It's not because of an ill intent on anyone's part; it is simply due to a lack of precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: You say that there is an establishment format for this form, and you say that thus there are 277 documents, which we see in the left corner, and there are 735 sheets. Who put in these figures actually?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: These two figures are written in by the clerk at the archives who received the documentation, and he adds up the figures including corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So it's only after all the corrections have been taken into account that the clerk puts in the total number of documents and sheets?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's when it's turned over to the archives. And this number, 21606 is written in by another clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to these two numbers, 277 and 735. Did I understand you correctly when you explained that this number, 277 documents, is the result of adding up all the numbers in the column "documents," column number 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And the sum of sheets is from the column number 6?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us some more. What about the same reference number on both documents, 21606, you say one document has the stamp of the archives, the other doesn't, although the number is the same. But there is another difference. One document states exactly what it is, whereas in another document a whole segment is pasted over.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody covered this column. I don't know why. Looking at other technical features, the number of pages and sheets, everything is identical. But what I don't understand is why one of these has the stamp of the military archive and the other doesn't. Now, who covered up part of this form, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 7 of the document on the left, and I think page 2 of the document on the right, archive unit 82. That's it. Can we just zoom in on 82 on the left and on the right. Let's see the columns 3, 4, 5, and 6. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Look at this now. In one archive unit, number 82, it says: "Official Note from the meeting of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff with the chief of the administration for the preparation of republican organs for defence in the Republic of Serbia, SMO." In both documents in columns 5 and 6 we see there are two documents. We see it was corrected in a way that differs from the corrections in other boxes, both above and below. In other boxes the correction is written on top of the original number, and here it's below the original number. Maybe -- maybe this is one document or maybe it's two documents. Can I -- can you give us your comment.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In column number 3 we see the name of the document archived under this item, official note from the meeting, et cetera. We see the number 248-1, as it is in our log-book. We see it's a document of three pages. Somebody, I don't know who, made this correction. They just changed the document -- the number of pages and sheets, and they wrote in the number of documents without writing a brief description.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they write the description? Were they supposed to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were supposed to. In addition, this number, 248-2, written in longhand is supposed to be written above the original number, if possible. And the handwriting is identical to the handwriting on the stamp on that order of the commander of the 3rd Army on resubordination that I did not understand the provenance of. That handwriting on the register stamp of the office and the handwriting here is the same. And if it's two persons, then these two persons are not authorised to do each other's job. From several aspects, this entry is problematic. I -- it leads me to believe that it must have been done at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask the usher or the Legal Officer to put back on the screen D585 in B/C/S alongside P888.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So please remember this number written in longhand 248-2. Let us look at the reference of this document. In the right top corner the document on the left is marked 248.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And in this correction it says that under item number 82 a document was entered marked 248-2. Is this the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back now to the archive list, the document we had on the screen a moment ago. That's it. D588. Can we now please go to the last page of both versions. Can we please scroll up a bit. You have a hard copy. We see something marked in column number 7, something was written in longhand and signed. There are certain corrections. It says in the signature "chief," with an indication "on behalf of the chief." What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Record made by the chief of office and it's signed by my deputy, Colonel Radoicic, on my behalf. There's nothing controversial there. On the right-hand side in column 7 the clerk at the archive Dusan Mladenovski, signed to indicate that it was he who received this documentation into the military archive. That means that he was the person who made the corrections on this sheet and no one else was authorised to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything noteworthy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we add up the number of documents and sheets, we will note that this number is no longer correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the -- in the form on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: If we just add it up. If we just add it up without taking into account corrections, then the number on the first page is still accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person who counted this obviously didn't know or failed to take into account the corrections and modify the number on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So documents D588 and D587, your tabs 15, 16 will be the documents we're going to look at again. I have the impression that the pages are not the same -- in fact, I'm sure they're not the same. D588 and D587. This is more like it. And the first page -- I don't think this is the first page. [In English] In fact, it's a log-book. That's correct now. [Interpretation] The document on the right should look the same, but it doesn't look the same. D588 and D587 I think are documents that were exhibited yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the right we should be looking at the same thing at the same heading as on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have to go to the second page of the document on the left I think to see the lower part of the document on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. Now can we have the same document in B/C/S, again one alongside the other, page 1. Correct, and on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Colonel, it's numbers 15 and 16. These are the originals of the one document and the other, I suppose. Now, the question is whether it's the same document. I think there are some obvious differences on the first page, on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first one was obtained from the military archive, the one on the left. And the document on the right is a copy -- I don't know where it comes from, but basically it's the same document, it's our log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where was it created?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of every year, our office opens a new log-book and we start entering documents for that year starting from number 1 as they come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does this log-book look like in technical terms? Does it provide for a decent level of security and protects the register against abuse?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a hard binding. The number of sheets is verified, and it's impossible to take out a page without leaving a visible trace. It should be sealed, but in this case we haven't done that because it is a hard-bound book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it allowed to make modifications and corrections in this book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Corrections are not even necessary, let alone allowed, if the procedure is followed. There is a procedure for entering documents and for following up on documents, so there is no need to correct anything at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who is responsible for the contents of this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Ultimately the chief of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That would be you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be me, but technically speaking it's the office manager whose direct responsibility it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see that document again, 248. Can we zoom in on the right-hand-side document. 248, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at entry number 248, that's the first column. We see two documents entered there with their dates, and we have columns 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 containing data. Could you please comment on what we can see here. For starters, because later on we'll stick to one document so as to follow through the entire 248 entry, can you tell us whether in your opinion the left and the right side of the document are identical. Is it the same document? Have a closer look and then share your conclusion with us.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The same?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in even further on the left-hand side document. Let's look at entry number 248. We can remove the right-hand side document, but before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, before that, the right-hand side part that we can see without any data, it's blank. Why is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever provided this document believed that that part of the page should be covered and that it wasn't necessary. This was done by technical means when photocopying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So the same explanation as with the archive list before?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's do what I proposed earlier then, to have the entry 248 zoomed in. Thank you. Very well. Please have a look at the monitor. It is document 248. In the archive list we can see that there was some data in columns 5 and 6, stating that there were two documents and five sheets, I believe. But it said that there was only one document, and here it is different. I'd like to hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Under 248 of the register of the office on the 15th of May a document was entered under number 1, strictly confidential, the federal defence ministry, the administration for Defence preparations, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document that was entered under 82?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, and it contains its full title there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: So entry 248, item 2, on the 26th of May, 1999, we have a document of the 3rd Army number 872-94/1-2. It seems that there is no link between the first and the second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Because under the rules sub-items are only added to those documents that they are in direct relation to. These should be documents dealing with the same issue, and it is only then that they are entered as items 1, 2, and 3 to the original number. That is to say the document from the Federal Ministry of Defence does not seem to have any relation to another document which is under number 2 coming from the 3rd Army. There should have been no reason to do that, and it corresponds to what we could see before according to the number of documents and sheets in the archive list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And your final conclusion is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That this could have only been entered subsequently, given the lack of expertise of those who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You have specifically document number 2 in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this was done illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at column number 6. We see that the number there is 872-94/1-2. It says "3rd Army command."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This should be the register number of the document where it was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's keep this number in mind, 872-94/1-2. Let's next have only D585 put on the screen which is your tab 9, and we will go back to this document later. This should suffice if we zoom in on that part. What can we see in the upper right-hand side corner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: We see the very same number, 248.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And on the left side?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There is stamp of the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the two documents that we could see on the screen previously, this is D588 and 587. In your binder these are tabs 15 and 16. Page 2, please. Any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding 248?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything else of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we have any further comments on the entire register of the office of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps concerning the linkage between documents. If there are two documents that are related, they should be under the same entry number with subnumbers. As you can see, for example, in 254 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please clarify that, and let's wrap it up for today.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 254 contains four documents, four subdocuments, but they are related. These were issues of status dealt by -- through the ministry and our department for recruitment and personnel issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about 248?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There we see no link between the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest we conclude for the day, Your Honours, given that we are -- ran out of time, and I will only require a short amount of time tomorrow morning concerning my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must now adjourn, and we resume at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
